### Basics

- [v] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [v] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Some editors' run/debug configurations only support adding additional args to the end of the command, but not before the command as a pipeline. In this case, to complete the redirection of stdin, it must be done at the end of the command

### Describe the solution you'd like

Such as VSCode's editor config ,It needs to provide the function of redirecting stdin at the end of the command. Not all extensions support redirecting stdin through the stdio field or modifying debug commands. In such cases, stdin redirection must be added to args
```json
    {
      "name": "Python",
      "type": "debugpy",
      "request": "launch",
      "program": "${file}",
      "python": "python",
      "args": [
        "<",
        "${workspaceFolder}/test/in.txt",
        ">",
        "${workspaceFolder}/test/out.txt"
      ],
      "console": "integratedTerminal"
    },
```
So I must use zsh or fish as debug console

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Adding the command `<i` or `<in` redirects stdin just like bash's `<`

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

When using Nushell as a login shell, if the `$env.PWD` value points to a non-existing directory (e.g. because the directory was deleted or moved), any built-in command will print duplicate errors:

```
/tmp/old-dir> ls
Error: nu::shell::error

  × $env.PWD points to a non-existent directory
  help: Use `cd` to reset $env.PWD into a good state

Error: nu::shell::error

  × $env.PWD points to a non-existent directory
  help: Use `cd` to reset $env.PWD into a good state

Error: nu::shell::error

  × $env.PWD points to a non-existent directory
  help: Use `cd` to reset $env.PWD into a good state

Error: nu::shell::error

  × $env.PWD points to a non-existent directory
  help: Use `cd` to reset $env.PWD into a good state
```

Depending on the command, I get either 4 or 5 duplicates. For instance, `ls` prints the error 4 times, and `pwd` prints it 5 times.

Note that running `cd` as instructed will also print an error:

```
/tmp/old-dir> cd
Error: nu::shell::error

  × $env.PWD points to a non-existent directory
  help: Use `cd` to reset $env.PWD into a good state

~>
```

### How to reproduce

From a Nushell login session:

1. `mkdir /tmp/old-dir`
2. `cd /tmp/old-dir`
3. `rm /tmp/old-dir`
4. `ls`


### Expected behavior

It would be a nice small usability improvement if the error could be printed only once.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

In Vi edit mode, if the cursor of the user is aligned on the letter `a` in the following example:

```
a.b.c
```

Pressing `e` will bring the user's cursor to the end of the word. Since Nushell's knowledge of a word is wrong, it will move the cursor to the letter `c` as if the user pressed `E` rather than `e`.

I think it is because the implementation of the Vi mode's concept of a "word" is not correct regarding the dot character.

Also, an interesting thing is that if the user's cursor is on the letter `c` and he then presses `b` to go to the beginning of the previous word, then he'll end up on the previous dot (one character to the left of `c`), which is correct.

There seems to be inconsistencies.

### How to reproduce

N/A

### Expected behavior

When in VI mode, using `w`, `e`, `ge` or `b` should jump between words relative to the cursor.

According to the Vim documentation,

> A word consists of a sequence of letters, digits and underscores, or a
> sequence of other non-blank characters, separated with white space (spaces,
> tabs, <EOL>).  This can be changed with the 'iskeyword' option.  An empty line
> is also considered to be a word.

The relevant part of the definition here is "other non-blank characters".

For e.g.,

```
a b c
```

This is 3 words while

```
a.b.c
```

this is 5 words as the two dots each count as a word. However,

```
...
```

This is a single word consisting of 3 times the character `.`.

Regarding the example given earlier with `a.b.c`. Pressing initially `e` when the cursor of the user is on letter `a` should bring the user's cursor to the first character `.`.

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

I think it would be beneficial to add configurable options to `explore` besides colors. Often when I use the command I find myself wishing I could modify just one keybind or tweak some behavior just a little.

### Describe the solution you'd like

*These are proposed solutions from my experience, It is likely and possibly best if they are modified to follow nushell convention if they are implemented*

## Quick reference
| option | choices | desc | reasoning |
| :--: | :--: | :-- | :-- |
| inline_preview | bool | preview a nested structure while navigating | Shows a short preview of a field instead of [list 1 item] etc, easier for scanning |
| keybinds | record of strings | allow customization of controls | lets the user decide how they are most comfortable navigating |
| peek-mode | cell-path, value, type | modify what `--peek` returns | lets user pick what they actually want returned |
| missing_value_symbol | string | change how missing values are displayed | this is in `table` configuration and should remain consistent for explore |
| horizontal scrolling | na | capture horizontal scrolls | key navigation can be slow |
| mouse capture | bool | select with click, descend with second | cursors are quicker, and sometimes preferred |

## Further notes
**inline_preview**
 - the expand (`e`) option does something similar, but this would be in the interactive menu as opposed to a static view mode
 - could be an integer to configure how many elements get shown
 - optionally make rows taller for more elements
 - indicate it's a preview with one or more:
   - text color
   - wrapping with structure syntax ( `[ ... ]` for lists. `{ ... }` for records, etc)
   - truncating with `...` or something else
 - similar to how `table -e` does it
 - could be something set on/off as by default and toggled via a keybind
 - should definitely have a sane limit for space and performance reasons

**keybinds**
 - examples (and my main wants): 
   - `esc` to hard exit
   -  `q` to go up a level
   - `space` to descend
 - supporting vim motions by default is great, but users should be able to choose
 - these would merge with the given defaults

**peek-mode**
 - this may be better as a `--peek` parameter with a default, that is a decision better made by the maintainers
   - if modifying the peek flag to take and argument, value would be kept as default for compatibility
 - returning the cell path in particular would be very useful to quickly find a piece of data and then access it in a pipeline
 - tying into the keybinds idea, `ctrl-x` could be bound to exiting and returning the value, while `ctrl-p` does the same for the cell path, etc

**missing data symbol**
- this would maintain consistency with table, of which explore is an interactive version
- may make more sense to just follow the table config value, or globalize it to `env.config.missing_data_display_symbol`

**scrolling**
- we already capture vertical scrolling, horizontal scrolling can be just as useful 
- feels really weird to not have it when using a trackpad

**mouse capture**
- one click: select cell
- click on select cell (and double click): descend just as enter
- in the same vein as horizontal scrolling, this would make mouse based navigation intuitive
- while I think it should just exist, this could be toggled for those who prefer clicks to only select text

## Example config
*ignoring pre-existing options*

**Complex inline_preview** (with placeholder options)
```nu
$env.config.explore = {
  inline_preview: {
    enabled: true
    max_items: 3           # how many list/record items to show
    expand_rows: false     # make rows taller to fit more preview content
    truncate_symbol: "…"   # symbol for truncated content
    show_structure: true   # wrap with [ ], { }, etc.
  }
  keybinds: { ... }
  peek_mode: "cell-path"
  missing_value_symbol: "∅"
}
```

**Simple inline preview**
```nu
$env.config.explore = {
  inline_preview: 3       # number of items to preview (0 = disabled)
  keybinds: { ... }
  peek_mode: "cell-path"
  missing_value_symbol: "∅"
}
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Not much to consider here besides a custom viewer AFAIK

### Additional context and details

These are all great quality of life features I would appreciate while using `explore`, but I defer to the community and maintainers to decide which features if any are worth implementing, and how they should be best implemented.

My personal ranking by importance (which I think mirrors implementation complexity):
1. keybinds
2. default symbol
3. peek mode
4. inline preview

*This is a pretty hefty wall of text, if it is better I am happy to split it into separate issues*

*Edit: added mouse and horizontal scroll, I meant to have these but it slipped my mind*

### Describe the bug

On macOS, when `nu` is launched through a Zsh **function** or **wrapper**, closing the terminal window directly (instead of exiting the shell manually) causes the `nu` process to hang and consume ~99% CPU.

This issue specifically occurs in the context of Zsh functions and does not appear when calling the binary directly or when using Bash as the host shell.


### How to reproduce

1. **Define a wrapper function** in a clean Zsh session:
```zsh
__nu() { command nu "$@"; }

```


2. **Launch Nushell** using the function:
```zsh
__nu

```


3. **Close the Terminal window** directly (e.g., clicking the 'X' button or `Cmd+W`) while the Nushell session is active.
4. **Check System Monitor:** Observe that a `nu` process remains active, consuming nearly 100% of a CPU core.


### Expected behavior

Expected: Clean process termination.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

When `$env.ENV_CONVERSIONS` gets modified with `load-env { ENV_CONVERSIONS: (...) }`, they are not applied to the current environment, despite https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/14591 making it seem like it should.

I have not tested changing it other than with `load-env` and direct assignment `$env.ENV_CONVERSIONS = (...)`, the latter of which works as expected.

Related:
- https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/14514
- https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/12904

### How to reproduce

1. Pick an environment variable to convert like `XDG_DATA_DIRS`
2. Set `ENV_CONVERSIONS` with something like:
   ```nushell
   use std/config env-conversions
   load-env { ENV_CONVERSIONS: { XDG_DATA_DIRS: (env-conversions).path } }
   ```
3. Notice `$env.XDG_DATA_DIRS` keeps it's original string value (`/some/path:/other/path`)

### Expected behavior

`ENV_CONVERSIONS` should apply whenever it's value changes, regardless of method used to change it

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

I noticed that PR #16285 fixed the issue regarding the cleanup of direct background jobs. However, I observed that job kill (and likely shell exit) only terminates the direct child process, leaving the grandchild process running as an orphan.

I am not sure if this is intended behavior or a bug

### How to reproduce

1. Spawn a job that involves a wrapper (creating a grandchild process):
 ```nu
 $ job spawn { nu -c "python3 -m http.server 9999" }
 46
 $ job list
╭───┬────┬────────┬───────────────╮
│ # │ id │  type  │     pids      │
├───┼────┼────────┼───────────────┤
│ 0 │ 46 │ thread │ ╭───┬───────╮ │
│   │    │        │ │ 0 │ 16044 │ │
│   │    │        │ ╰───┴───────╯ │
╰───┴────┴────────┴───────────────╯
 ```

2. **Before Killing:** Observe the process tree.
   *   The wrapper `nu` process (PID 16044) is the direct child.
   *   The `python` process (PID 16059) is the grandchild (`ppid` is 16044).

```nu
 # Check the wrapper (Direct Child)
 $ ps --long | where pid == 16044
 # Result:
╭───┬───────┬───────┬──────┬────────┬──────┬─────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────┬─────╮
│ # │  pid  │ ppid  │ name │ status │ cpu  │   mem   │ virtual  │                       command                       │ sta │ ... │
│   │       │       │      │        │      │         │          │                                                     │ rt_ │     │
│   │       │       │      │        │      │         │          │                                                     │ tim │     │
│   │       │       │      │        │      │         │          │                                                     │ e   │     │
├───┼───────┼───────┼──────┼────────┼──────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────┼─────┤
│ 0 │ 16044 │ 95331 │ nu   │ Sleep  │ 0.00 │ 18.7 MB │ 445.7 GB │ /opt/homebrew/bin/nu -c python3 -m http.server 9999 │ a m │ ... │
│   │       │       │      │        │      │         │          │                                                     │ inu │     │
│   │       │       │      │        │      │         │          │                                                     │ te  │     │
│   │       │       │      │        │      │         │          │                                                     │ ago │     │
╰───┴───────┴───────┴──────┴────────┴──────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────┴─────╯


 # Check the Grandchild
 $ let py_pid = (lsof -ti :9999 | into int)
 $ ps --long | where pid == $py_pid
╭───┬───────┬───────┬────────┬────────┬──────┬─────────┬──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────╮
│ # │  pid  │ ppid  │  name  │ status │ cpu  │   mem   │ virtual  │                         command                         │ ... │
├───┼───────┼───────┼────────┼────────┼──────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────┤
│ 0 │ 16059 │ 16044 │ Python │ Sleep  │ 0.00 │ 25.5 MB │ 445.7 GB │ /opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.2/Frameworks/Pyth │ ... │
│   │       │       │        │        │      │         │          │ on.framework/Versions/3.14/Resources/Python.app/Content │     │
│   │       │       │        │        │      │         │          │ s/MacOS/Python -m http.server 9999                      │     │
╰───┴───────┴───────┴────────┴────────┴──────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────╯
 
```

3. **Action:** Kill the job.
 ```nu
 $ job kill 46
 ```

4. **After Killing:** Observe the result.
   *   The wrapper `nu` (PID 16044) is successfully terminated.
   *   **BUT**, the `python` process (PID 16059) persists and has been re-parented to init (PPID 1).

 ```nu
 # Check Child
 $ ps --long | where pid == 16044
╭────────────╮
│ empty list │
╰────────────╯
 # Check GrandChild
 ps --long | where pid == $py_pid
 # Result:
╭───┬───────┬──────┬────────┬────────┬──────┬─────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────╮
│ # │  pid  │ ppid │  name  │ status │ cpu  │   mem   │ virtual  │                         command                          │ ... │
├───┼───────┼──────┼────────┼────────┼──────┼─────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────┤
│ 0 │ 16059 │    1 │ Python │ Sleep  │ 0.00 │ 25.5 MB │ 445.7 GB │ /opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.2/Frameworks/Pytho │ ... │
│   │       │      │        │        │      │         │          │ n.framework/Versions/3.14/Resources/Python.app/Contents/ │     │
│   │       │      │        │        │      │         │          │ MacOS/Python -m http.server 9999                         │     │
╰───┴───────┴──────┴────────┴────────┴──────┴─────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────╯
 ```

### Expected behavior

When a background job is terminated (either via job kill or by exiting the shell), both child and grandchild process should be killed

body_text:
## Problem

When creating errors with the new `src` field (added in 0.110.0), the external file information is not accessible in the JSON serialization when catching errors. This makes it difficult to programmatically access the file path and other `src` metadata.

## Current Behavior

When you create an error with `src` field:

```nu
error make {
  msg: 'Code block not found'
  label: {
    text: 'No nushell code block found'
    span: {start: 0, end: 10}
  }
  src: {
    name: 'example.md'
    text: $content
    path: '/path/to/example.md'
  }
}
```

And then catch it:

```nu
try {
  # ... error make above
} catch {|err|
  print ($err.json | from json)
}
```

The JSON output contains:
- `msg`
- `labels`
- `code`
- `url`
- `help`
- `inner`

But **NOT** the `src` field data (name, text, path).

The file path is only visible in the `debug` field as a string:
```
"NamedSource { name: \"example.md\", source: \"<redacted>\", ..."
```

## Desired Behavior

The `src` field data should be included in the JSON serialization, for example:

```json
{
  "msg": "Code block not found",
  "labels": [...],
  "code": "nu::shell::outside",
  "src": {
    "name": "example.md",
    "path": "/path/to/example.md"
    // Note: 'text' could be omitted for brevity
  },
  ...
}
```

## Use Case

When building tools that use `error make` with external files (like markdown processors, config validators, etc.), it's useful to programmatically access the source file path from caught errors for:
- Logging which file had the error
- Re-reading the file to provide additional context
- Building error reports that reference the source file
- Chaining errors with file information preserved

Currently, the only way to access this information is parsing the `debug` string, which is fragile.

## Related

- The `src` field feature was added in #17129
- Related to general catch closure information: #9248, #16253

### Bug report form

### Describe the bug

A bit of background - I am trying to set a variable if it is not set yet. How to determine whether it is set already? For record fields, I can use something like `$rec.field = $rec.field? | default -e default_value`.  This does not work for variables. Any attempt to reference non-existing variable produces compile time error. The next best thing I found is `scope variables`. But it also has issues.

When a variable is overshadowed (i.e. defined with `let` several times) in a script, `scope variables` command does not seem to see it until after the last `let`.

### How to reproduce

Put the following commands in a script file:

```nu
let FMT_VER = 'initial_value'
print -e $FMT_VER                    # the variable FMT_VER can be used  
scope variables | print -e           # but `scope variables` does not see it yet !!!!

let FMT_VER = scope variables | where name == '$FMT_VER' | get -o 0.value | default -e default_value
print -e $FMT_VER                    # because `scope variables` does not work (yet), the initial value is not preserved
scope variables | print -e           # after the second assignment, `scope variables` can finally see it
```

Then execute the file. This is what I get:

```

### Describe the bug

When trying to convert unix epoch with milliseconds using `into datetime -f "%s%3f"` I get the following error: `can't convert bad or unsupported format string to could not parse as datetime using format '%s%3f'`. Worth mentioning, that format `%s%.3f` work fine.



It seems like a bug because using the same format string to format a date works as expected. Here is some output with unexpected behavior

> date now | format date "%s%3f"
1769503677954

Error: nu::shell::cant_convert

 1 │ date now | format date "%s%3f" | into datetime -f "%s%3f"

   ·                                        ╰── can't convert premature end of input to could not parse as datetime using format '%s%3f'
   ╰────

> '1769503677.954' | into datetime -f "%s%.3f"
27/01/26 08:47:57

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

When listing files with Nushell `ls`, the `mode` field does not reflect the presence of POSIX ACLs (the `+` marker shown by coreutils `ls -l`). This makes `ls | select name mode` misleading for permission auditing and scripting, because a file can have extended ACLs but Nushell still displays the mode as if it were plain POSIX bits.

I’m trying to use Nushell to inspect permission state, and I need a visual/scriptable indication that extended ACLs are present.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add feature parity with coreutils `ls` by including an ACL indicator in the displayed mode string when ACLs are present.

Specifically: when a file has extended ACLs, the mode should be displayed with a `+` suffix (e.g. `rw-rw-r--+`, `drwxrws---+`), matching the common `ls -l` convention.

Example of desired output:

```

❯ ls -la /srv/mqtt/db | select name type mode
╭───┬────────────────────────────┬──────┬────────────╮
│ # │           name             │ type │   mode     │
├───┼────────────────────────────┼──────┼────────────┤
│ 0 │ /srv/mqtt/db/mosquitto.db  │ file │ rw-rw-r--+ │
╰───┴────────────────────────────┴──────┴────────────╯

```


### Describe alternatives you've considered

Use external `ls`/`stat` instead of Nushell for permissions (works, but defeats the point of using structured `ls` output in pipelines).

### Additional context and details

On this system, coreutils `ls` accurately indicates ACL presence with `+`:

```

❯ ^ls -la /srv/mqtt/db
total 24
drwxrws---+ 2 svc-mqtt svc-mqtt  4096 Jan 27 18:43 .
drwxrws--x+ 5 svc-mqtt svc-mqtt  4096 Jan 24 17:32 ..
-rw-rw-r--+ 1 svc-mqtt svc-mqtt 13656 Jan 27 18:43 mosquitto.db

```

But Nushell does not:

```

❯ ls -la /srv/mqtt/db | select name type mode
╭───┬───────────────────────────┬──────┬────────────╮
│ # │           name            │ type │   mode     │
├───┼───────────────────────────┼──────┼────────────┤
│ 0 │ /srv/mqtt/db/mosquitto.db │ file │ rw-rw-r--  │
╰───┴───────────────────────────┴──────┴────────────╯

```

Also note that structured output in JSON loses the ACL indicator entirely:

```

❯ ls -la /srv/mqtt/db | get name mode user group | to json
[
[
"/srv/mqtt/db/mosquitto.db"
],
[
"rw-rw-r--"
],
[
"svc-mqtt"
],
[
"svc-mqtt"
]
]

```

This is problematic because the on-disk permission state includes extended ACLs, but Nushell’s `mode` field suggests a plain mode-only permission model.

body_text:
### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

`gstat` returns `-1` for all fields and `no_repository` when the git repository uses the `reftable` ref storage format (available in 2.45+). 
This is because `gstat` uses libgit2, which doesn't seem to have format reftable support



### How to reproduce

1. migrate local git project to reftable format:
  `git refs migrate --ref-format=reftable`
1. Run `gstat` whilst in the repository:
    ```sh-session
    $ gstat
    ╭─────────────────────┬───────────────╮
    │ idx_added_staged    │ -1            │
    │ idx_modified_staged │ -1            │
    │ idx_renamed         │ -1            │
    │ ...                 │ -1            │
    │ repo_name           │ no_repository │
    │ branch              │ no_branch     │
    ╰─────────────────────┴───────────────╯
    ```


### Expected behavior

I expected the `gstat` command to work with reftable format 🤷 or have a callout that said format isn't supported yet

### Configuration

| key                  | value                                                                                     |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| version              | 0.110.0                                                                                   |
| major                | 0                                                                                         |
| minor                | 110                                                                                       |
| patch                | 0                                                                                         |
| branch               |                                                                                           |
| commit_hash          | d40e191d8efad32a174d85b2a45f7ba4796cff84                                                  |
| build_os             | macos-aarch64                                                                             |
| build_target         | aarch64-apple-darwin                                                                      |
| rust_version         | rustc 1.90.0 (1159e78c4 2025-09-14)                                                       |
| rust_channel         | 1.90.0-aarch64-apple-darwin                                                               |
| cargo_version        | cargo 1.90.0 (840b83a10 2025-07-30)                                                       |
| build_time           | 2026-01-18 02:18:55 +00:00                                                                |
| build_rust_channel   | release                                                                                   |
| allocator            | standard                                                                                  |
| features             | default, mcp, network, plugin, rustls-tls, sqlite, static-link-openssl, trash-support     |
| installed_plugins    | gstat 0.108.0, query 0.110.0, semver 0.11.9, skim 0.15.0                                  |
| experimental_options | example=false, reorder-cell-paths=true, pipefail=false, enforce-runtime-annotations=false |

NOTE: the output above says `gstat` is `0.108` for some reason but running this command shows otherwise (a bug?):

```sh-session
$ nu_plugin_gstat  -h
Nushell Plugin
Encoder: msgpack
Version: 0.110.0
Plugin file path: /Users/mkatychev/.cargo/bin/nu_plugin_gstat

Command: gstat
Description:
 > Get the git status of a repo

Flags:
  -h, --help: Display the help message for this command
  --no-tag: Disable git tag resolving

Parameters:
  (optional) path <path>: path to repo
======================
```

### Workaround


1. Prune stale remote refs (reduces potential conflicts):
  `git remote prune origin`
1. macOS/Windows(?): check for case sensitive conflicts (this triggered the issue), return refs that duplicate

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Use cases:

- Passing file references to tools that only accept URIs.
- Generating clickable links in terminal output (e.g. using [`ansi link`](https://www.nushell.sh/commands/docs/ansi_link.html)).
- Emitting stable, shareable identifiers in logs/structured output.

There are various [`path`](https://www.nushell.sh/commands/docs/path.html) and [`url`](https://www.nushell.sh/commands/docs/url.html) helpers but there doesn't appear to be a built-in, cross-platform way to convert a filesystem path into a valid `file:` URI as defined by [RFC 8089](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8089).

This is especially error-prone on Windows due to:

- Drive-letter paths (`C:\...` -> `file:///C:/...`)
- UNC paths (`\\server\share\...` -> commonly `file://server/share/...`)
- Correct percent-encoding (spaces, `#`, etc.) without encoding `/` path separators.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Enable path <-> `file:` URL conversion by allowing the structured outputs of existing commands to compose:

```nu
'C:\Users\me\a b.txt' | path parse | url join
'file:///C:/Users/me/a%20b.txt' | url parse | path join
```

- `url join` accepts structured path records (from `path parse`). If the input record/table matches the `path parse` schema, `url join` should:
   - reconstruct the path (as `path join` would)
   - emit a canonical `file:` URL string
   - percent-encode the URL path component correctly (spaces -> `%20`, etc.)
   - handle Windows drive paths (`file:///C:/...`) and UNC (`file://server/share/...`) consistently
- `path join` accepts URL records (from `url parse`). If the input record matches `url parse` output and `scheme == 'file'`, `path join` should:
   - percent-decode the URL path
   - convert to the platform-native local path
   - support UNC (`file://server/share/...` -> `\\server\share\...` on Windows)

The path -> URL direction auto-expands relative paths to absolute without following symlinks.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- `path from-uri`/`url from-path`
- `into uri`/`into path`
- `format uri` with `path join` learning the conversion

### Additional context and details

Proper UNC path support can come later if it makes the initial feature simpler to deliver.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

**Platform** tested with nixos-24.11 and nushell 0.100.0
**Terminal software** Gnome Console + picocom/screen 

When logging into eg an embedded device over an FTDI (serial console over USB), nushell has a weird bug where it's almost totally unresponsive, and it has a slight blink each and every 2 seconds roughly. bash works fine in the same circumstances. I tried to change the $TERM env value before running it (tried "xterm", "dumb"), it lagged just the same.

I'm very sorry I didn't use a more recent nushell, my system is not upgradeable as it is so it's the best I can have now. I can retry with a static build on request. I doubt the symptoms will change though.

I sometimes have garbage output on stdout, like : 
```
~> [24;1R[24;4Rl[24;4R[24;10R[24;10R[24;17R[24;17R[24;23R[24;23R[24;30R[24;30R[24;37R[24;44R[24;51R[24;58R[24;58R[24;65R[24;65R[24;72R[24;72R[24;79R[24;79R[24;6R[24;6R[24;13R[24;13R[24;20R[24;20R[24;27R[24;27R[24;34R[24;34R[24;41R[24;41R
```
$TERM value may influence the presence of that garbage output, but I can't check easily, since once it's stuck on FTDI I need to hard-reboot it, and I don't want to mess with the eMMC too much.

## Observations
- The 2 seconds blink makes me think it could be related to [this reedline issue](https://github.com/nushell/reedline/issues/1010)
- #14474 could also be related
- my embedded device is a Radxa Zero, but I don't think that's relevant
- a sample run :

**Warning: may require you to hard-reboot the target machine.**

**Platform** tested with nixos-24.11 and nushell 0.100.0
**Terminal software** Gnome Console + picocom/screen 

When logging into eg an embedded device over an FTDI (serial console over USB), nushell has a weird bug where it's almost totally unresponsive, and it has a slight blink each and every 2 seconds roughly. bash works fine in the same circumstances.   for n in 1..($count) {

### How to reproduce

```nushell
# Run from a directory with a lot of old releases, with nu_releases being set to a selection of those subdirectories
kv get nu_releases
| each {|release|

    let closure_script = r#'
      use std bench
      def sum-to [count: int] {
        1..($count) | reduce {|it,sum| $in + $it }
      }
      bench { sum-to 1000 } | reject times?
    '#
    let closure_bench = (run-external  $"($release.name)/nu" "-c" $closure_script)

    let for_script = r#'
      use std bench
      def sum-to [count: int] {
        mut sum = 0
        for n in 1..($count) {
          $sum = $sum + $n
        }
        $sum
      }
      bench { sum-to 1000 } | reject times?
   '#

    let for_bench = (run-external  $"($release.name)/nu" "-c" $for_script)

    { release: $release.name reduce: $closure_bench for: $for_bench  }
  }
| 
| insert release_num { $in.release |  str replace -r 'nu-0\.([^\.]*).*' '$1' | into int }
| sort-by release_num
| reject release_num
```

### Expected behavior

I haven't bisected this down to a particular change in 108, and I'm sure that it was probably a good change overall. Just want to see if anything can be done to get back to the previous performance, as that seems like a pretty big (33%'ish) hit.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

```
~ $ nu
Error:   × I/O error: Function not implemented (os error 38)
```

Config: Nothing in `.config/nushell`, which is a symlink to `nushell` directory in my dotfile.

If i remove `.config/nushell` and run `nu`, it works perfectly, but the produced config also contains nothing but comments.

Symlinks work fine on Linux and macOS.

It seems it's because Nushell on Termux doesn't respect symlink. Other CLI tools on Termux work fine when using symlinks for their configs.

### How to reproduce

- Install termux (https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.termux/).
- `pkg install nushell`
- Create an empty directory anywhere.
- Create a symlink as `~/.config/nushell` pointing to that empty directory.

### Expected behavior

Nushell starts correctly.

~ $ nu --version

### Related problem

I was recently made aware of the package [Tirith](https://github.com/sheeki03/tirith), which prevents IDN Homograph attacks. I was wondering if it made sense to implement that directly into Nushell. Or something similar to it. 

### Describe the solution you'd like

Maybe make it only run on HTTP Requests so it just runs through a known table of homographs and rejects the http request flat if it includes them with a warning. Make it overridable with an extra parameter so that one can explicitly opt in while aknowledging its dangerous.  

```# Blocked by default
> http get https://аpple.com
Error: Potential homograph attack detected
  × URL contains lookalike characters
   ╭─[input:1:1]
 1 │ http get https://аpple.com
   ·              ───┬──
   ·                 ╰── 'а' (Cyrillic U+0430) looks like 'a' (Latin)
   ╰────
  help: Use --allow-homographs to proceed anyway

# Explicit opt-in
> http get https://аpple.com --allow-homographs
# Warning displayed but request proceeds
```

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

I can send a doc PR, but let's see first if we agree that this is a bug and that it's specifically a documentation bug.

Having just started with nushell, I was configuring my `$env.config.buffer_editor`. Looking at https://www.nushell.sh/book/configuration.html, it gives these examples:

```
$env.config.buffer_editor = "code"
# or
$env.config.buffer_editor = "nano"
# or
$env.config.buffer_editor = "hx"
# or
$env.config.buffer_editor = "vi"
# with args
$env.config.buffer_editor = ["emacsclient", "-s", "light", "-t"]
# etc.
```

I had one question that I find this did not quite answer about the required semantics `buffer_editor`: Does something in nushell expect it to block and exit only when the editing is done? (Maybe the answer is obvious to a veteran user.)

The examples here point two ways: nano, hx, vi and `emacsclient -t`, I believe, do block. `code`, on the other hand, at least on my Linux box, does not; it opens the file either in a new or existing window and immediately exits.

This is in contrast with `doc_config.nu` which does specifically list `code --wait` as a command that can be used—although I think that's wrong in another way: It claims you can use the string `"code --wait"`, while at least on my computer the only way to pass command line arguments to editors in `buffer_editor` is to give it a list:

https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/4436f58ccf9dcbee412045d90526bf091e29a930/crates/nu-utils/src/default_files/doc_config.nu#L102-L107

```
> $env.config.buffer_editor = "code --wait"
> config nu
Error: nu::shell::external_command

  × External command failed
   ╭─[entry #25:1:1]
 1 │ config nu
   · ────┬────
   ·     ╰── `code --wait` not found
   ╰────
  help: Failed to find the editor executable
```

So I read the code. Here it seems the code clearly expects `buffer_editor` to block:

https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/4436f58ccf9dcbee412045d90526bf091e29a930/crates/nu-cli/src/repl.rs#L465-L476

### How to reproduce

See above

### Expected behavior

Here's my take:

It seems `buffer_editor` blocking is likely inherent to the design of nushell.

While I was hoping to be able to say `config nu` and continue using the shell while editing the config, it seems to me this is not how things work, and probably it's best to fix the documentation to be explicit about the editor needing to block. I can use  `job spawn { config nu }` instead, which would break if the editor used the terminal, then—maybe in theory there could be a separate `non_blocking_buffer_editor`?.

This being the case, I would suggest these fixes:

1. In https://www.nushell.sh/book/configuration.html:
  a. Change it to *not* use `code` as an example, but change that to `[code, --wait]` or possibly `[code, --wait, --new-window]`.
  b. Add an explicit mention that the editor must only exit after the editing is done.
2. In https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/4436f58ccf9dcbee412045d90526bf091e29a930/crates/nu-utils/src/default_files/doc_config.nu#L102-L107,
  a. Fix the wording to not suggest the string `"code --wait"` since that doesn't work
  b. Add an explicit mention that the editor must only exit after the editing is done

### Describe the bug

I can send a doc PR, but let's see first if we agree that this is a bug and that it's specifically a documentation bug.

Having just started with nushell, I was configuring my `$env.config.buffer_editor`. Looking at https://www.nushell.sh/book/configuration.html, it gives these examples:

```
$env.config.buffer_editor = "code"
# or
$env.config.buffer_editor = "nano"
# or
$env.config.buffer_editor = "hx"
# or
$env.config.buffer_editor = "vi"
# with args
$env.config.buffer_editor = ["emacsclient", "-s", "light", "-t"]
# etc.
```

I had one question that I find this did not quite answer about the required semantics `buffer_editor`: Does something in nushell expect it to block and exit only when the editing is done? (Maybe the answer is obvious to a veteran user.)

The examples here point two ways: nano, hx, vi and `emacsclient -t`, I believe, do block. `code`, on the other hand, at least on my Linux box, does not; it opens the file either in a new or existing window and immediately exits.

This is in contrast with `doc_config.nu` which does specifically list `code --wait` as a command that can be used—although I think that's wrong in another way: It claims you can use the string `"code --wait"`, while at least on my computer the only way to pass command line arguments to editors in `buffer_editor` is to give it a list:

https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/4436f58ccf9dcbee412045d90526bf091e29a930/crates/nu-utils/src/default_files/doc_config.nu#L102-L107

```
> $env.config.buffer_editor = "code --wait"
> config nu
Error: nu::shell::external_command

  × External command failed
   ╭─[entry #25:1:1]
 1 │ config nu
   · ────┬────
   ·     ╰── `code --wait` not found
   ╰────
  help: Failed to find the editor executable
```

So I read the code. Here it seems the code clearly expects `buffer_editor` to block:

https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/4436f58ccf9dcbee412045d90526bf091e29a930/crates/nu-cli/src/repl.rs#L465-L476

### How to reproduce

See above

### Expected behavior

Here's my take:

It seems `buffer_editor` blocking is likely inherent to the design of nushell.

While I was hoping to be able to say `config nu` and continue using the shell while editing the config, it seems to me this is not how things work, and probably it's best to fix the documentation to be explicit about the editor needing to block. I can use  `job spawn { config nu }` instead, which would break if the editor used the terminal, then—maybe in theory there could be a separate `non_blocking_buffer_editor`?.

This being the case, I would suggest these fixes:

1. In https://www.nushell.sh/book/configuration.html:
  a. Change it to *not* use `code` as an example, but change that to `[code, --wait]` or possibly `[code, --wait, --new-window]`.
  b. Add an explicit mention that the editor must only exit after the editing is done.
2. In https://github.com/nushell/nushell/blob/4436f58ccf9dcbee412045d90526bf091e29a930/crates/nu-utils/src/default_files/doc_config.nu#L102-L107,
  a. Fix the wording to not suggest the string `"code --wait"` since that doesn't work
  b. Add an explicit mention that the editor must only exit after the editing is done

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

```
mkdir src/a
mkdir src/b
mkdir src/c

cd a<TAB><enter>
```

Pressing tab triggers completion, with a single option of "src/", and "rc/" is properly appended to the input.

But, it also opens the menu, which redraws with new results after the input is changed. This leaves "src/a" selected, so hitting enter picks it.

This is very frustrating. I expect that series of key presses to leave me in the "src" directory, but I end up in whatever child it happens to pick. 

### How to reproduce

```
mkdir src/a
mkdir src/b
mkdir src/c

cd a<TAB><enter>
```

### Expected behavior

It should complete up to "src/" when the tab is pressed and accept that input when enter is pressed.

Instead the menu is active, so enter selects the first menu item which is "src/a" because the menu redrew.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

I attempted to install and run nushell on Windows on ARM64. Installation completed, but the app doesn't run from Windows Terminal. I get a dialog box with this message:

> nu.exe - System Error
> The code execution cannot proceed because VCRUNTIME140.dll was not found. Reinstalling the program may fix this problem.

I tried installing the [Microsoft Visual C++ v14 Redistributable (ARM64)](https://aka.ms/vc14/vc_redist.arm64.exe) and ran Nushell again, and it brought up the same error message.

Note that this is only when I run Nushell from Windows Terminal directly, from its new tab menu. If I run nu.exe from PowerShell or Command Prompt, even when running those from Windows Terminal, it runs fine. It also runs directly from File Explorer.

I don't know why a Rust application would need the C++ runtime, but that's probably the closest equivalent to libc on Windows.  This might be a bug in Windows Terminal, or in the profile created in Windows Terminal by the Nushell installation.

This problem doesn't occur on Windows on x64.

### How to reproduce

`winget install nushell --scope machine`

Then open Windows Terminal, and attempt to open a new tab with the Nushell profile from the dropdown.


### Expected behavior

Just run with no dialog box looking for VCRUNTIME140.dll.

### Describe the bug

When using table --collapse on input containing multiple records with nested list values, rows are rendered incorrectly. Specifically, values from a previous record appear in the collapsed output of a subsequent record, causing misalignment between columns.

* I also test it on current main branch of nushell

### How to reproduce

### Using --expand
[[a b]; [1 [2 2]] [3 [4 4]]] | table --expand

| a | b |
| ---- | ---- |
| 1 | 2 |
|   | 2 |
| 3 | 4 |
|   | 4 |


### Using --collapse:
[[a b]; [1 [2 2]] [3 [4 4]]] | table --collapse


| a | b |
| ---- | ---- |
| 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 2 |
|   | 4 |
|   | 4 |


### Expected behavior

| a | b |
| ---- | ---- |
| 1 | 2 |
|   | 2 |
| 3 | 4 |
|   | 4 |

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Given a script file `sample.nu`
```nu
def main [--test (-t): string] {
  print $test
}
```

Invoking `nu sample.nu -t value` yields
```
value
```

There are some applications that parse option values after shorthand flags even if they follow the flag directly with no whitespace separation.

- `nu sample.nu -t value`
- `nu sample.nu -tvalue`

[clap](https://docs.rs/clap/latest/clap/) is a prominent example of a library that does this by default. ([playground](https://play.rust-lang.org/?version=stable&mode=debug&edition=2024&gist=393a84e7c9c7a105eef277f2970005fa))

In nu this is an error, because it presumes that the following letters are also flags and then prevents user error.

`nu sample.nu -tvalue` yields
```
Error: nu::parser::only_last_flag_in_batch_can_take_arg

  × Only the last flag in a short flag batch can take an argument.
   ╭─[<commandline>:1:7]
 1 │ main -tvalue
   ·       ┬
   ·       ╰── only the last flag can take args
   ╰────
```



### Describe the solution you'd like

During argument parsing, when encountering a short-hand option that requires a value, parse it from the remaining text.

To a script expecting a value to a flag `-t` those invocations would be equivalent
- `nu sample.nu -t value`
- `nu sample.nu -tvalue`

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context and details

It seems that this would only break backward compatibility for invocations that weren't correct in the first place. However it could be confusing to users that expect to set an additional flag, but end up providing a value to a prior flag instead.

The long form parsing does essentially the same (only `=` separated), so there's already code that can parse the value from inside the same argument.

body_text:
### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [ ] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Sometimes you need to use sudo/sudo-rs with a command, sometimes with an alias, and that does not work.

Having to re-specify with sudo is not a very nice or clean way to have it set. There is a lot of alias set in the alias file that I use.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add support to any alias to be run with sudo/sudo-rs.

Having this would be a diferential to other shells, since they do not have the support. At least not directly. That I know of.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I know alternative ways that would make it work, but it requires different rewrites or code dups, not a nice experience.

### Additional context and details

Perhaps nushell could read the alias, parse that command, add sudo if sudo comes as prefix to it.

---

There is this case.

https://github.com/trifectatechfoundation/sudo-rs

> You can work around that by creating e.g. an alias, but that will only change your own invocations of sudo to sudo-rs and not affect other programs and scripts that use sudo.

I guess this would need consideration also for other users. 

I was using it as alias, however I changed it to [symlink](https://github.com/trifectatechfoundation/sudo-rs/issues/1478), and that might be a better option to not replace sudo.

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Nushell treats all environment variables as case-sensitive, and has #17558 made this more consistent on all platforms.
Unfortunately, as #14551 correctly notes, this goes against the Unix convention and POSIX (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/V1_chap08.html).

As also noted in that issue, this becomes particularly problematic when multiple variables that only differ in casing are present. Personally, it caused me a decent amount of headache just now to figure out why `$env.SHELL` is suddenly modified when loading a Nix devShell using direnv.

### Describe the solution you'd like

It would therefore be great to have a way of defining/assigning env vars in a case-respecting manner. That means at minimum not coercing an assignment to `shell` into an assignment to the existing variable `SHELL`, and ideally allowing two variables that only differ in casing (such as `SHELL` and `shell`) to coexist.

It might be implemented in the form of a special flag for `load-env` and similar commands.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Ideally, I would love to be able to turn off case-insensitivity entirely, since I see little benefit (beyond Windows compatibility, which is not relevant for my use case) and believe it only causes more issues and annoying edge cases.

But as Nushell seems to have committed to case insensitivity I assume such a toggle would be difficult to realize and would probably cause a bunch of incompatibility between scripts etc.

- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Nushell treats all environment variables as case-sensitive, and has #17558 made this more consistent on all platforms.
Unfortunately, as #14551 correctly notes, this goes against the Unix convention and POSIX (https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/V1_chap08.html).

As also noted in that issue, this becomes particularly problematic when multiple variables that only differ in casing are present. Personally, it caused me a decent amount of headache just now to figure out why `$env.SHELL` is suddenly modified when loading a Nix devShell using direnv.

### Describe the solution you'd like

It would therefore be great to have a way of defining/assigning env vars in a case-respecting manner. That means at minimum not coercing an assignment to `shell` into an assignment to the existing variable `SHELL`, and ideally allowing two variables that only differ in casing (such as `SHELL` and `shell`) to coexist.

It might be implemented in the form of a special flag for `load-env` and similar commands.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Ideally, I would love to be able to turn off case-insensitivity entirely, since I see little benefit (beyond Windows compatibility, which is not relevant for my use case) and believe it only causes more issues and annoying edge cases.

But as Nushell seems to have committed to case insensitivity I assume such a toggle would be difficult to realize and would probably cause a bunch of incompatibility between scripts etc.

### Describe the bug

Originally reported [here](https://github.com/nushell/nushell/pull/17917#issuecomment-4169901563).

```nushell
> ast -f 'ps o>'
╭─content─┬───────shape────────┬─────span──────╮
│ ps      │ shape_internalcall │ ╭───────┬───╮ │
│         │                    │ │ start │ 0 │ │
│         │                    │ │ end   │ 2 │ │
│         │                    │ ╰───────┴───╯ │
│ o>      │ shape_garbage      │ ╭───────┬───╮ │
│         │                    │ │ start │ 3 │ │
│         │                    │ │ end   │ 5 │ │
│         │                    │ ╰───────┴───╯ │
╰─────────┴────────────────────┴───────────────╯

> ast -f 'ls o>'
╭─content─┬───────shape────────┬─────span──────╮
│ ls      │ shape_internalcall │ ╭───────┬───╮ │
│         │                    │ │ start │ 0 │ │
│         │                    │ │ end   │ 2 │ │
│         │                    │ ╰───────┴───╯ │
│ o>      │ shape_globpattern  │ ╭───────┬───╮ │
│         │                    │ │ start │ 3 │ │
│         │                    │ │ end   │ 5 │ │
│         │                    │ ╰───────┴───╯ │
╰─────────┴────────────────────┴───────────────╯
```

The reason is that without a file expression, `o>` and other redirection tokens `out+err>` etc, are treated like normal tokens, and parsed as command arguments, instead of an incomplete redirection expression.

Described already.

Parsed as a "special" redirection expression with filename missing.

- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

I use `$nu.user-autoload-dir` pretty extensively with a lot of small files to easily manage stuff like completions and isolated functions.

I'd like to organize them a bit more by separating them into subfolders, but nushell makes it quite difficult to actually source an entire directory (for the same reasons the user autoload directory even exists IIRC)


### Describe the solution you'd like

I'd like the mechanism for autoload (or at least the one for users ?) to recursively walk through the autoload directory and subdirectories and load every .nu file found.


### Describe alternatives you've considered

The main alternative as far as I know is just dealing with the flat structure with longer filenames.

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

Similar to: https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/13786

I was trying to calculate a percentage and did 

```
> 54/(54+127)
Error: nu::shell::external_command

  × External command failed
   ╭─[repl_entry #8:1:5]
 1 │ 54/(54+127)
   ·     ───┬──
   ·        ╰── Command `54+127` not found
   ╰────
  help: `54+127` is neither a Nushell built-in or a known external command
```

I couldn't understand why this didn't work:
- https://www.nushell.sh/book/types_of_data.html#integers has some examples of expressions, and mine look similar
- https://www.nushell.sh/book/operators.html#order-of-operations describes that parenthesis can be used for grouping

I had to open the issue tracker and search for "parenthesis" to find an issue where someone was running into the same problem.

Only then did I realize blank space was the problem. `54 / (54 + 127)` is valid, any missing blank space makes it fail.

I feel like Nushell should be able to understand my intent rather than trying to run a command. I don't think people are trying to run commands like `54+127` or `54/181`. 



### Describe the solution you'd like

In order of preference, perhaps one of:
- when the expression is a valid arithmetic expression (or the type is a number), interpret it as such?
- if it fails with a missing command error try again as arithmetic?
- update the help string in the output to suggest adding blankspace if the expression looks like math?
- updating the getting started documentation to point this out clearly?

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context and details

### Describe the bug

It's not possible to write to `stdout` or `stderr` and then process input line by line. Consider the following:

``` nu
def main [] {
    print --stderr "Interpreter listening..."
    lines | each { str reverse | print }    
    print --stderr "Interpreter done."
}
```

The idea to use `lines` like this comes from #14901. I've also tried using `input` in a loop, but I can't figure out how to terminate it on EOF.

### How to reproduce

Save the above script as `sample.nu`. Then run it:

``` shell-session
$ nu --stdin sample.nu
Interpreter listening...
Interpreter done.
```

It exits without waiting for the input. Then comment out the first `print` statement, run it again and see it working correctly.

### Expected behavior

The script should print to `stderr`, then wait for input. Each input line should be immediately printed in reverse. Pressing `ctrl-d` (or closing the input stream piped from another process) should result in the closing message being printed. After that the script should terminate without any error.

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

According to the [Documentation](https://www.nushell.sh/book/working_with_lists.html#iterating-over-lists) `get` is the correct way to obtain items from lists. 
Consider following code:
```nu
let pids = [1234,2345,131313]
let selected_index = '1' # output of external program, so it happens to be a string
$pids | get $selected_index
```
This will throw en error in line three as `get` assumes the input to be a table as I (unknowingly)  passed a string as the argument. 
Even though it is an easy fix using `into int`, the error states that that it cannot find the column '1'. 
This is quite confusing as the input is clearly a list.
I would like that getting items from a list at a specific index is more clearly separated from getting named columns.

### Describe the solution you'd like

I propose one or more of the following options:
**1.**
Making the error massage differ based on its input value. E.g.: "List cannot be indexed with string"
**2.**
Changing  `get`s behavior to attempt converting the input value to an `int` when the input value is a list.
However might make its usage more confusing as it already has a certain table/list duality, by being used with both. 
**3. (preferred)** 
Introducing a new 'at' (or whatever named) builtin which exclusively gets items from lists 
and fails with an appropriate error message in case the index is not an int or the input is not a list. 
This is intentionally supposed to be more restrictive to make the usage more obvious.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

I have a requirement to load a custom SQL COLLATION as my Nushell application processes data from an sqlite database with its data encoded with it.  Currently the nushell's sqlite_utils has not way to load collation sequences even though it is a standard feature of sqlite clients.   Additionally, Rust supports it, per:

Rusqlite: Use the create_collation method on the [rusqlite::Connection](https://docs.rs/rusqlite/latest/rusqlite/struct.Connection.html) object. This method takes a name and a closure that compares two strings, returning a std::cmp::Ordering.

I think its likely many Nushell sqlite_utils users will benefit from this feature.  If you need more information for my specific use case, I need to better handle processing of foreign characters.  My only work around currently is to NOCASE everything, which reduces data fidelity.   Specifically, if this feature is implemented, I will be loading https://github.com/mooredan/unifuzz

Thank you for your consideration.

### Describe the solution you'd like

see above

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Use of NOCASE in SQL statements - reduces data fidelity.
- Client-side Unicode folding in Nu for selected queries - Diacritic-correct for DISTINCT/sort post-processing; can't fix WHERE/JOIN
- Nu plugin nu_plugin_rmsqlite (Rust, raps rusqlite + ports RMNOCASE) - silly when sqlite_utils is a comprehensive solution.
- Shell out to a helper (Python/Node) for fidelity-critical queries - Awkward boundary; runtime dep; latency

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

On supporting terminals, the output of `ls` command can be clicked, and the items will be launched with defualt programs. My educated guess is that since ls command adds the source metadata to its output, the default printing functionality has some special processing for the output of `ls` that wraps file names into `ansi link`.

Would it be possible to have something like that for the output of `glob` command?

### Describe the solution you'd like

Like in `ls`: if the output of `glob` is piped to another command, it is just a list of strings. If displayed, the strings are wrapped in `ansi link` where feasible.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

`glob * | each { ansi link }` would work.

But the whole idea here is convenience, making the work with nushell smoother. So it would be nice if this worked out of the box...

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

When you create and cd into an empty directory and execute `ls .*`, the following gets written to stdout:
```
╭───┬──────┬──────┬───────┬──────────╮
│ # │ name │ type │ size  │ modified │
├───┼──────┼──────┼───────┼──────────┤
│ 0 │ ..   │ dir  │ 636 B │ now      │
│ 1 │      │ dir  │   0 B │ now      │
╰───┴──────┴──────┴───────┴──────────╯
```

This is unexpected, since the correct result would be to show both the ".." and the "." directories, but instead the latter one is rendered empty.

When executing `ls /.*` from the same directory, the "." folder is printed correctly:
```
╭───┬───────────┬──────┬────────┬──────────────╮
│ # │   name    │ type │  size  │   modified   │
├───┼───────────┼──────┼────────┼──────────────┤
│ 0 │ /..       │ dir  │  154 B │ a day ago    │
│ 1 │ /.        │ dir  │  154 B │ a day ago    │
╰───┴───────────┴──────┴────────┴──────────────╯
```

### How to reproduce

1. mkdir /tmp/test123
2. cd /tmp/test123
3. ls .*
4. ls /.*
5. Notice how in the table rendered after the former command the "." folder is invisible.

### Expected behavior

The dot folder should always be visible when the ".." folder is visible.

### Basics

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

This is similar to #16851, but the resolution of that ticket only addresses half the ticket.

It's quite common to want to write a little wrapper for an http querying tool to supply defaults for a specific API, like e.g. an authentication token. These defaults typically apply to all methods.

Unfortunately, since the `http` command's methods are literal nushell subcommands, they cannot be assigned by variable, and the top-level `http` command just "intelligently" infers the method (AIUI, `POST` whenever a body is given, `GET` otherwise).

This has caused me to write this ridiculous thing:

```nu
match $method {
  delete => ($body | http delete --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
  get => ($body | http get --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
  head => ($body | http head --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
  options => ($body | http options --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
  patch => ($body | http patch --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
  post => ($body | http post --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
  put => ($body | http put --headers {X-API-Key: $api_key} $'http://($address)($path)')
}

# Nevermind the use of `http` with authentication here; this is all on localhost, for better
# or for worse, I still need to consider the security story here. It's not entirely unlikely that
# I'll start generating openssl certs for the sake of it, but that's completely unrelated to 
# nushell.
```

I would like to not write this ridiculous thing.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Can we either have the method not be determined by subcommand but by value, and/or have a flag on the top-level command to set the method?

### Describe alternatives you've considered

The ridiculous match block you see above, not using nushell's built-in `http` command and falling back to `curl`, suggesting something uber-fancy like a generic http client builder based on reqwest, or writing a plugin that does that.

### Additional context and details

- [x] I have done a basic search through the issue tracker to find similar or related issues.
- [x] I have made myself familiar with the available features of Nushell for the particular area this enhancement request touches.

### Related problem

The `save` built-in requires an explicit file path that is sometimes known which occasionally leads to long commands.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Similar to the alternative idea in https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/18291, make `save` not require an argument when the input has such metadata. For example, I would expect the following to use the `filename` directive within a [Content-Disposition](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition) header to derive the default filename:

```
http get $url | save
```

Also, it would be nice if it printed the path when it wasn't supplied explicitly so you could extend the pipeline to use the file (e.g. perform some work then `rm`) rather than having the final operation be the `save`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context and details

This would be one less motivating reason for https://github.com/nushell/nushell/issues/16082

### Describe the bug

When running `history session` in the REPL init script, it always outputs `0`. Only after the REPL is available can we use the same command to get the _actual_ ID.

### How to reproduce

1. Edit `$nu.config-path`
2. Add `print (history session)`
3. Observe: on startup, it prints `0`

### Expected behavior

The correct history session should be shown immediately.
I understand that this may be due to the history not being initialized yet, in which case the command should return `null`, or even better, throw an error stating it should not be called during initialization. The docs should reflect this.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

I don't know if I should report it rather here or to GNOME. I use Nushell as the default shell, and, previously, Nushell sometimes reported that there is an error in config, but everything worked. Recently, I turned the computer on, and, when I logged in to GNOME, it returned me to gdm.

So I was looking for the error, and found that, if I remove the Nushell configuration (config.nu), it works. So the bug is most likely between GNOME and Nushell when Nushell reports an error. This was not an issue previously, so I don't know what changed so it stopped working.

This is the config file which caused that (with changed name extension because of GitHub):
[config.nu.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28499771/config.nu.txt)
It shows these errors:
```
Error: nu::shell::invalid_config

  × Encountered 2 error(s) when updating config

  × Unknown config option: $env.config.filesize.metric
     ╭─[/home/matj1/backup/nushell/config.nu.txt:221:17]

 221 │         metric: false # true => KB, MB, GB (ISO standard), false => KiB, MiB, GiB (Windows standard)
     ·                 ──┬──
     ·                   ╰── remove this

     ·                 ───┬──

### Related problem

I encountered this while testing my `git status` porcelain parser, in particular when parsing quoted paths.
I made a test repository with files using the `touch` command. I wanted to test special characters, including ASCII control characters.
Then I ran the following pipeline `gitx status | insert ls { |r| ls $r.path }` and noticed that one particular file with only control chars (named `"\u{1}\u{2}\u{3}\u{4}"`) resulted in the current directory listing. This is #6315.

Then I noticed another problem: **the `ls` command escapes paths**.
From what I checked, all other commands outputting filenames leave the path as is, but `ls` is different.

```
> ls
╭───┬──────────────────────┬──────┬──────┬───────────────╮
│ # │         name         │ type │ size │   modified    │
├───┼──────────────────────┼──────┼──────┼───────────────┤
│ 0 │ \u{1}\u{2}\u{3}\u{4} │ file │  0 B │ 2 hours ago   │
│ 1 │ ala ma kota          │ file │  0 B │ 3 hours ago   │
│ 2 │ asdsfdsf             │ dir  │ 60 B │ 9 minutes ago │
│ 3 │ gaba"laba            │ file │  0 B │ 3 hours ago   │
│ 4 │ iłoł                 │ file │  0 B │ 3 hours ago   │
│ 5 │ ą\u{2} fd            │ file │  0 B │ 2 hours ago   │
│ 6 │ ą fd                 │ file │  0 B │ 2 hours ago   │
│ 7 │ ą ę                  │ file │  0 B │ 3 hours ago   │
╰───┴──────────────────────┴──────┴──────┴───────────────╯
```

This breaks scripting:

```
> ls | select name | insert my-type { |r| $r.name | path type }
╭───┬──────────────────────┬─────────╮
│ # │         name         │ my-type │
├───┼──────────────────────┼─────────┤
│ 0 │ \u{1}\u{2}\u{3}\u{4} │         │
│ 1 │ ala ma kota          │ file    │
│ 2 │ asdsfdsf             │ dir     │
│ 3 │ gaba"laba            │ file    │
│ 4 │ iłoł                 │ file    │
│ 5 │ ą\u{2} fd            │         │
│ 6 │ ą fd                 │ file    │
│ 7 │ ą ę                  │ file    │
╰───┴──────────────────────┴─────────╯
```

### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like for the escaping to happen in a different place, preferably with a metadata tag, like what's used to color paths.
Then it could be applied to other commands take return path, as well as custom commands (like the one I made).

It could be integrated into `path_columns` metadata, or more generally some other metadata, like `escape_string: true`, `escape_columns: [...]`, etc. for other kinds of strings.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context and details

`ls` escapes paths in all modes: `--long`, `--short-names`, `--full-paths`.

From what I checked, all other commands outputting filenames leave the path as is, but `ls` is different.

```

╰───┴──────────────────────┴──────┴──────┴───────────────╯
```

This breaks scripting:

```
> ls | select name | insert my-type { |r| $r.name | path type }

│ 7 │ ą ę                  │ file    │
╰───┴──────────────────────┴─────────╯
```

### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like for the escaping to happen in a different place, preferably with a metadata tag, like what's used to color paths.
Then it could be applied to other commands take return path, as well as custom commands (like the one I made).

It could be integrated into `path_columns` metadata, or more generally some other metadata, like `escape_string: true`, `escape_columns: [...]`, etc. for other kinds of strings.

### Related problem

Wouldn't it be cool to have uniform binding/variable declaration/definition syntax for binding/variable definitions, command parameters, record entries, etc? Apart from being more consistent, it would be also more familiar for users comming from other shells (bash/ksh) that also uses `=` for separating associative array keys and values and it would even allow to inline type entries of record literals which is currently not possible AFAIK. Another use would be faster refactoring of a set of variables into a record, which I do quite often.

### Describe the solution you'd like

1. function parameters `[var[: type][ = default]]` -- no change
2. binding definition `let var[: type][ = value]` -- no change
3. record entries `{ key1[: type] = value key2[: type] = value2 }` -- `=` instead of `:` which would allow using `:` as a separator for optional type

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

When I use `def --env` in Nushell, calling `cd` updates `$env.PWD` and `pwd`, but the underlying OS process working directory (as observed via `pwdx`) doesn't immediately change during execution of the function body.

This leads to cases where external tools (e.g. `udisksctl`) report a mounted filesystem as “busy”, because the Nushell process still has its working directory inside the mount point, despite `cd` appearing to have moved it.

Workaround:
Using an external shell forces cwd isolation:

^sh -c "cd / && udisksctl unmount -b /dev/sdX"

### How to reproduce

1. Create a mount point (USB or loop device), e.g. /dev/sdb1 mounted at /media/test

2. cd /media/test

3. Run this Nushell function from /media/test/:

def --env test [] {
    cd $env.HOME
    print $"env PWD: ($env.PWD)"
    print $"nushell pwd: (^pwd)"
    print $"pid: ($nu.pid)"
    input "Press Enter after checking with pwdx in another terminal and trying to unmount"
}

3. While the function is running, in another terminal:

pwdx <nu_pid>

When I did this, the process working directory was still inside the original mount path.

4. Attempt unmount while test is still running:

udisksctl unmount -b /dev/sdX

### Expected behavior

I expect after I `cd` inside `def --env`, the Nushell process should not still be holding an active working directory on the previous path in a way that prevents filesystem unmounting.

### Describe the bug

When I use `def --env` in Nushell, calling `cd` updates `$env.PWD` and `pwd`, but the underlying OS process working directory (as observed via `pwdx`) doesn't immediately change during execution of the function body.

This leads to cases where external tools (e.g. `udisksctl`) report a mounted filesystem as “busy”, because the Nushell process still has its working directory inside the mount point, despite `cd` appearing to have moved it.

Workaround:
Using an external shell forces cwd isolation:

^sh -c "cd / && udisksctl unmount -b /dev/sdX"

### How to reproduce

1. Create a mount point (USB or loop device), e.g. /dev/sdb1 mounted at /media/test

2. cd /media/test

3. Run this Nushell function from /media/test/:

def --env test [] {
    cd $env.HOME
    print $"env PWD: ($env.PWD)"
    print $"nushell pwd: (^pwd)"
    print $"pid: ($nu.pid)"
    input "Press Enter after checking with pwdx in another terminal and trying to unmount"
}

3. While the function is running, in another terminal:

pwdx <nu_pid>

When I did this, the process working directory was still inside the original mount path.

4. Attempt unmount while test is still running:

udisksctl unmount -b /dev/sdX

### Expected behavior

I expect after I `cd` inside `def --env`, the Nushell process should not still be holding an active working directory on the previous path in a way that prevents filesystem unmounting.

### Bug report form

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

Firstly, upon running something like `[] | insert 0.0 1`, instead of getting the expected nested lists containing a 1 (`[ [ 1 ] ]`), similarly to how it works on records - `{} | insert a.0 1` returns `{a: [1]}`.

Secondly, on an empty list, the error message itself contains an underflowed number.

This can have an easy fix for just the underflow in the error message - using `saturating_sub` instead of just the minus operator during the construction of the error message (or better, explicitly checking for empty lists with a more descriptive error message) OR a harder fix, that is to fix the inconsistency between the creation of a new nested list/record using the insert command on a list input vs a report input.

I am willing to make the change, as I have stumbled upon this while working on another PR related to the insert command.

Please also note that this issue is also present for the `upsert` command as well

### How to reproduce

`[] | insert 0.0 1` or `[] | insert 0.a 1`

returns this error:

```
Error: nu::shell::access_beyond_end

  × Row number too large (max: 18446744073709551615).
   ╭─[repl_entry #23:1:13]
 1 │ [] | insert 0.0 1
   ·             ┬
   ·             ╰── index too large (max: 18446744073709551615)
   ╰────

```

### Expected behavior

A list containing a list with one element - `[ [ 1 ] ]` or a list containing a record with the specified mapping - `[ { a: 1} ]`.

If neither of those behaviours, then at least a properly constructed error message

- [x] I have done a basic search of the issue tracker to find any existing issues that are similar.
- [x] I have checked that my version is at least the latest stable release available via my installation method.

### Describe the bug

nushell currently supports at least 3 variations of newline-delimited JSON inputs. First, there is `from json --objects`. There's also [jsonl](https://jsonlines.org/) and [ndjson](https://github.com/ndjson/ndjson-spec) support in stdlib.

### How to reproduce

See `from json` having an `--objects` flag:

```
from json --help
...
  Parse a stream of line-delimited JSON values.

{ "b": 2 }' | from json --objects
  ╭───┬────┬────╮
  │ # │ a  │ b  │
  ├───┼────┼────┤
  │ 0 │  1 │ ❎ │
  │ 1 │ ❎ │  2 │
  ╰───┴────┴────╯
```

See stdlib functions for newline-delimited JSON support:

```
nu -c "
  use std
  scope commands
  | where name =~ '^std formats from '
